summary: Monsoon Mixtape is an interactive web application that converts twenty years of NASA climate data (2006-2025) into a song of about one minute, performed on traditional Malaysian instruments. Users select a location on the map, and the application plays the climate history of that place. Temperature determines the melody, rainfall is represented by kompang and gendang drums, humidity controls the amount of echo, and haze muffles the seruling flute. Unusual months are marked by the sound of a gong. Using NASA POWER data from 46 locations across Malaysia, the project shows that every location became warmer, with an average increase of about 0.66°C. This can be heard as the melody rises and the gong sounds more frequently towards the end of the song. The project responds to the challenge of turning Earth science data into sound. This matters because climate numbers are difficult to picture, and audio, captions and keyboard control allow blind and low-vision users, students and other interested people to explore them. The use of Malaysian instruments also makes the data feel more relevant to local users
details:
Introduction

Malaysia lies on the equator, so it has no winter or summer. Climate change here does not arrive as a dramatic change of seasons. It appears as gradual shifts in temperature, rainfall and haze, especially across the monsoon seasons. NASA provides data that can show these changes, but charts and maps are difficult to read for many people, including those with visual impairments. Monsoon Mixtape addresses this by turning 20 years (2006-2025) of NASA climate data for any location in Malaysia into a short song, so users can hear environmental change instead of only seeing it.

Methodology

The application was built with Python, FastAPI and Uvicorn for the backend, Flutter web and JavaScript for the interface, and Tone.js with the Web Audio API for sound. Climate data comes from the NASA POWER Monthly Point API.

We developed it in four steps:

  1. Data collection: We collected monthly climate data from 2006 to 2025 for the selected location.
  2. Data analysis: The backend calculates anomalies, z-scores and historical trends to find unusual months.
  3. Sound mapping: Climate variables are translated into musical parameters such as pitch, drum rhythm, reverb and instrument texture.
  4. Testing: We tested the application on different browsers and mobile devices to check performance, audio synchronisation and controls.

The data-to-sound mapping:

  • T2M (temperature): higher temperature gives higher melody notes
  • PRECTOTCORR (rainfall): heavier rain gives busier kompang and gendang patterns
  • RH2M (humidity): higher humidity gives more reverb and echo
  • AOD_55 (haze): more haze gives a more muffled seruling flute
  • Unusual months: marked by gong strikes, and bigger anomalies ring a bigger gong

The lead instrument depends on the region: sape for Sarawak, rebab for Kelantan and gamelan for other regions.


Results

The prototype shows that multi-year environmental data can be turned into sound. Audio playback matches the visual changes with minimal delay, different instruments represent different environmental patterns, and the visuals, audio, rhythm stage and narration together make an engaging learning experience. It also gives another way to explore Earth science beyond visual displays.

Discussion

We checked 46 locations across Malaysia, and every one became warmer, by about 0.66°C on average. For almost every location, 2024 was the hottest year. Very hot months rose from 4 in 2006-2015 to 421 in 2016-2025. In the song, this is heard as the melody rising and the gong ringing more often towards the end.

Rainfall changed unevenly. Most places became wetter, with some parts of Johor receiving up to 56% more rain, while some parts of Sabah and Sarawak became drier. Most places receive much more rain during the Northeast Monsoon from November to March (The Star, 2026). Haze appeared in short bursts, especially in 2015 between August and October, which is heard as the flute becoming muffled.

These results matter because most people find numbers hard to picture, and hearing the climate of their own town on Malaysian instruments makes it easier to understand and remember. Sonification can also help blind and low-vision people explore science (Zanella et al., 2022).

Limitations: First, NASA POWER data covers areas of about 50 km, so it misses small local differences such as highlands and coasts. Second, 20 years is shorter than the 30 years normally used to define a climate “normal” (World Meteorological Organization, 2017), which may make recent changes look slightly bigger than they are. Third, turning data into music involves design choices, and compressing 20 years into one minute hides some detail.

USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

We used artificial intelligence only as a tool to help build the project. The application itself does not contain any AI model. All sounds, captions and results come from NASA data and rule-based code, and the narration is made from simple Python templates filled with numbers from the data. The application does not need API keys or paid AI services.

We used Claude, an AI assistant made by Anthropic, to help with:

  • Code development: writing and debugging the FastAPI backend, the NASA POWER data pipeline, the Tone.js sound engine and the Flutter interface
  • Sound and data design: thinking through how data could be mapped to sound
  • Accessibility: adding keyboard controls, screen-reader labels and captions

Our team decided the idea, the way data is turned into sound, and the choice of Malaysian instruments. We ran and tested all the code that Claude suggested and listened to the output to check that it matched the data. All numbers come from our own analysis of NASA data.

SPACE AGENCY DATA

  • NASA Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) Project, Monthly Point API (https://power.larc.nasa.gov/), 2006-2025, queried at 46 locations across Malaysia on a 0.5° grid
  • No data from other space agencies was used.

OTHER DATA AND TOOLS

  • Map: OpenStreetMap contributors (https://www.openstreetmap.org/)
  • State boundaries: geoBoundaries, gbOpen MYS ADM1, licensed under ODbL 1.0 (https://www.geoboundaries.org/)
  • Sound: Tone.js, MIT license (https://tonejs.github.io/)
  • Map display: Leaflet, BSD-2-Clause license (https://leafletjs.com/)
  • Backend: FastAPI, MIT license (https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/)
  • Interface: Flutter (https://flutter.dev/)
